title: Irish Man Charged With Destroying U.S. Military Plane Becomes Protest Symbol
author: Miranda Jeyaretnam
body:
An Irish man has been charged in the U.S. with wielding an axe and using chemicals to destroy an American military plane in what supporters have described as a protest against the U.S. military.

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan accused 48-year-old Daithí O’Corrain of damaging a $60 million U.S. Air National Guard aircraft while it was parked at Ireland’s Shannon airport in April. O’Corrain allegedly cut hydraulic lines, smashed cockpit gauges, and poured ball bearings into the fuel tanks of the plane, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday.

O’Corrain is not in U.S. custody and his arraignment has not been scheduled. He was arrested by Irish police after the April 11 incident. He faces one charge in the U.S. of destruction of government property, and three charges in Ireland of trespassing, causing criminal damage to the perimeter fence at the airport, and causing criminal damage to the plane. If convicted, the U.S. charge carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

“These charges send a clear and powerful message that attacks on U.S. military assets—and thus our national security—will not be tolerated,” U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement.

A group of public supporters has rallied around O’Corrain, characterizing his actions as a political protest against the U.S. war with Iran and military aid to Israel. An online fundraiser described him as an “independent peace activist” and called the incident “an inspiring act of direct action … to resist the unwanted presence of the U.S. Military in Ireland.” Anti-nuclear, anti-war newspaper The Nuclear Resister reported in August that activists attended his court hearings in Ireland. Social media accounts made in support of O’Corrain posted information about solidarity protests and argued that the aircraft’s presence violated Irish rules governing foreign military aircraft. The Irish government has said that U.S. military aircraft landing in Ireland are subject to conditions, including restrictions on carrying arms without permission, and that missions aren’t launched from the airport.

O’Corrain has not made any public statements and is not known to be involved in any activist groups behind earlier protests at the airport, including when President Donald Trump visited in September.

Here’s what to know about the charges.

Prosecutors say O’Corrain planned for months

According to the indictment, O’Corrain breached the airport’s security perimeter at around 4:39 a.m. local time and entered the aircraft by breaking its rear crew door’s locking mechanism. He then covered the plane’s windows, except those in the cockpit, barricaded himself inside, and placed ball bearings mixed with epoxy into the plane door tracks to block them from being opened, the indictment alleges.

O’Corrain is alleged to have cut wire bundles and hydraulic lines, crimped a liquid oxygen line, destroyed the gauges in the cockpit, and punctured the plane’s air ducts. At around 9:40 a.m., the flight crew saw O’Corrain escaping out of a roof hatch before striking the plane with an axe and pouring unknown substances and ball bearings into the plane’s fuel tanks, according to the indictment.

Prosecutors alleged that O’Corrain had planned for months to break into the airport and damage the aircraft, including searching online about the construction of the C-130 Hercules aircraft and for coordinates for where to breach the airport’s security perimeter. The plane, a quad-engine turboprop that is mainly used for military transport, was parked on the airport’s taxiway while en route to a military assignment in another country.

Prosecutors also alleged that O’Corrain ordered capsules of a corrosive chemical, gallium, online, subscribed to a flight-tracker app, and attempted to contact a person who had been arrested in connection with a prior breach at the airport. He demonstrated “detailed knowledge” of the layout of the aircraft and how to destroy its critical components without compromising his safety, the indictment said, adding that he knew in advance the aircraft would be there.

“This was not an act of spontaneous vandalism,” said James Barnacle, head of the FBI’s New York office.

Anti-war protests at Shannon Airport

Shannon Airport has been the site of multiple protests against what critics describe as Ireland’s role in allowing U.S. military flights and troop transport through the airport. Protesters have argued that the U.S.’s involvement in various wars, particularly ongoing ones in Iran and Gaza, conflicts with Irish military neutrality.

According to Gaza’s Health Ministry, Israel has killed more than 74,000 people in Gaza since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack on southern Israel, which killed around 1,200 people in Israel and saw about 250 others taken hostage. In the absence of independent monitoring on the ground, the ministry is the primary source for casualty data relied upon by humanitarian groups, journalists, and international bodies. Its figures do not differentiate between civilians and combatants and cannot be independently verified by TIME. An investigation by The Guardian estimated that 83% of Palestinians killed in Gaza were civilians as of May 2025, citing data from the Israel Defense Forces.

In April 2017, Dan Dowling, then 35, and Edward Horgan, then 71, entered a restricted area and wrote “Danger, danger, do not fly” in red marker on a U.S. Navy aircraft. They were arrested in Ireland, and the jury heard in court that the markings were wiped off before the plane flew onward to a U.S. base in the Middle East.

“If you want my motivation, it is the killing of children in Iraq, Syria, Afghanistan and Yemen,” Horgan told reporters at the time, calling their action an “informative protest” to highlight that U.S. military aircraft were not being searched. He said he had handed Irish police at the airport a 35-page-long list of 1,000 children killed in conflicts involving the U.S. in the Middle East, Asia, and Africa.

Both men were acquitted of criminal damage in 2023, but convicted of trespass. Earlier this month, Ireland’s Supreme Court overturned Dowling’s trespass conviction. His attorney argued that the men believed their actions were necessary to protect lives.

On March 10, 2024, pro-Palestinian activists held a sit-in inside the terminal calling for an end to U.S. weapons transfers through Ireland.

Later that month, three pro-Palestinian activists approached a U.S. military aircraft carrying a Palestinian flag and a banner that read, “U.S. military out of Shannon.” They sat near the plane in an attempt to stop it from taking off. The activists were arrested and charged. Their trial was adjourned in February pending the Supreme Court ruling in Dowling’s appeal.

Galway Palestine Solidarity Campaign organizer Rania Muhareb told Irish newspaper The Journal that the activists were protesting “in line with a long tradition of Irish anti-war activism at Shannon.”

Around 500 people held another protest in support of Palestinians in April 2024 at the airport entrance, while a smaller group blocked the access road.

In May 2025, three people were arrested for driving a van through the airport’s perimeter fence in what was reported as a pro-Palestinian protest. In a separate incident that month, three women allegedly entered the runway and spray-painted the nose of a plane of Omni Air, a civilian airline that transports U.S. military personnel. Irish broadcaster RTÉ reported that the plane was not engaged in military activity. The women were arrested and charged with criminal damage and trespass, which they denied.

That November, three people were charged over allegedly entering the airfield and spray-painting a U.S. Navy Reserve Boeing 737 parked at Shannon. Their stated objection was that U.S. military use of Shannon violated Irish neutrality and supported Israel’s war in Gaza.

Hundreds of protesters also gathered near Shannon Airport during President Donald Trump’s visit to Ireland in September, chanting “U.S. military out of Shannon.”
